clue.text: Matilda is one avoiding bottom smack

indicators.note: in a down light the bottom is the final letter, and avoiding it means leaving that letter out

parts.note: Roald Dahl's Matilda is the central female character of her story

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl dodging a spanking on her backside.
explanation.walkthrough: HEROINE loses its last letter to give HEROIN. 'Smack' looks like a slap, but here it is slang for the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Smack is long-standing street slang for the opiate drug, so the two words name the same narcotic.

clue.text: Team spending time with forceps struggling to secure delivery

indicators.note: struggling letters writhe about and end up in a new order
spending something means using it up, so that letter is gone from the word

parts.note: taken as written
T is the standard abbreviation for time
taken as written

explanation.surface: A medical team wrestling with forceps to bring a baby safely into the world.
explanation.walkthrough: TEAM drops its T, and the leftover EAM is mixed with FORCEPS. The surface is a birth, but 'delivery' here is rescue.
explanation.definitionFit: To secure your delivery from a place or danger is to get yourself out of it, which is what breaking away achieves.

clue.text: Big Bird and Elmo have reinvented rearing beginners

indicators.note: a horse rearing rises up on its hind legs, so in a down light the letters run upwards
beginners are the opening letters of each of the words that come before

parts.note: the first letter of each of these four words

explanation.surface: Two Sesame Street puppets have come up with a new approach to bringing up children.
explanation.walkthrough: Big Bird and Elmo are Sesame Street characters, which makes 'Big Bird' look like part of the puppet scene rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhea is a large flightless South American bird, related to the ostrich and emu, so literally a big bird.

clue.text: European school ends up English instead

indicators.note: in a down light, going up means those letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for European

indicators.note: the ends of a word are its outermost letters, first and last

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A school on the Continent winds up teaching English in place of something else.
explanation.definitionFit: Used after a word like 'something' or 'somewhere', the adverb means other or in place of the thing named.

clue.text: Served as girl with best-in-class upside-down cake?

parts.note: W is a standard abbreviation for with
A1 means first-rate, written with the letter I for the figure one

indicators.note: turning a down light upside down makes its letters read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a cake can be served as a pudding course

explanation.surface: A girl brought out a top-of-the-class pineapple upside-down cake.
explanation.walkthrough: Upside-down cake is a real dessert, so 'upside-down' hides as part of its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A waitress is a woman who serves at table, so to work in that role is to have served as a girl in a café.

clue.text: Bring home outspoken little playmate for Eric

indicators.note: something outspoken is said out loud, so the sound is what counts

parts.note: Eric Morecambe's comedy partner was Ernie Wise, whom he called by the short form Ern

explanation.surface: A child loudly asking to bring a small friend home for their brother Eric.
explanation.walkthrough: Morecambe and Wise were a much-loved British comedy double act; Eric's pet name for his partner Ernie was Ern.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring home the bacon is to make a wage, so bringing home money is the idiom for earning it.

clue.text: Enthusiastically try putting baby Oscar in dress

indicators.note: putting one thing in something else places it inside, with the dress as the outer layer

parts.note: a gown is a long dress
a tot is a small child
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Eagerly having a go at getting little Oscar into his outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enthusiastically try' looks like an instruction to the child's dresser, but the whole phrase is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to town on something is the idiom for doing it with great energy and lavish effort, holding nothing back.

clue.text: Sister's half-siblings?

indicators.note: only half of the word is kept, here its second four letters

parts.note: brothers are male siblings

explanation.surface: A puzzle about a sister's half-brothers and half-sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-siblings looks like a family term, but 'half' is an instruction: keep the back half of BROTHERS.
explanation.definitionFit: The possessive pronoun stands in for 'belonging to her', just as 'Sister's' marks something owned by a female.

clue.text: Strip cartoon bear charged with a noisy disturbance

parts.note: to hull is to strip off an outer covering, as with strawberries
taken as written
Baloo is the bear in Disney's The Jungle Book

explanation.surface: A cartoon strip in which a bear is arrested for making a racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strip cartoon' reads as a comic strip, but 'Strip' is a verb on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A hullabaloo is a commotion or uproar, an outbreak of loud and confused noise.

clue.text: Composition from boy with a talent (though not fast)

indicators.note: 'though not' asks for the word with a second word taken out of it

parts.note: a son is a boy
taken as written
taken as written
Lent is the Christian period of fasting

explanation.surface: A piece written by a gifted lad, played at a slow tempo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not fast' sounds like a tempo marking, which suits the music; in fact it removes LENT from TALENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonata is a musical work, usually in several movements, for one or two instruments.

clue.text: Grew upward round about 10, then 10 to get muscle

indicators.note: going round something encloses it, so the following letters sit inside
going upward reverses the reading direction, so the letters are taken backwards

parts.note: rose is the past tense of rise, to grow higher
X is the Roman numeral for ten
the number written as a word

explanation.surface: A growth chart: the line climbed past ten and then hit ten again.
explanation.walkthrough: The two 10s give two different spellings: the Roman X and the word TEN, both inside ESOR.
explanation.definitionFit: An extensor is any muscle whose contraction straightens or extends a limb, the opposite of a flexor.

clue.text: Trouble brewing close to infant nurse

indicators.note: something brewing is stirred up and in ferment, so the letters are mixed
the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something is going wrong near the nurse who is looking after a baby.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrest is disturbance or agitation, often of a political kind, which is what trouble in a society amounts to.

clue.text: Capacity of rough partner in child's play to get body for rugby league

parts.note: rough and tumble is a fixed pairing

indicators.note: the second item gets the first, taking it inside itself

parts.note: the Rugby Football League governs the sport in England
a U-certificate show is one rated universal, fit for a child to see

explanation.surface: Rough-and-tumble games among children toughen them up for rugby.
explanation.walkthrough: Rough-and-tumble is children's play, so the first part reads as all one picture. U is the British film and theatre rating for material suitable for all ages.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumblerful is the amount a drinking glass holds, so it is a measure of capacity.

clue.text: Go 'CRASH!' Not quite what you might say playing with baby

definitions.text: what you might say playing with baby

indicators.note: not quite all of the word is wanted, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: to go is a euphemism for passing water
a comic-book sound for an explosion or crash

explanation.surface: A toddler's sound-effect game: shouting 'crash!' while playing with the baby.
explanation.walkthrough: KABOOM loses its M.
explanation.definitionFit: Peekaboo is the game of hiding your face and popping out, and the word itself is what you call to the infant.

clue.text: First 60% of Indian bread rolls to become baby food?

indicators.note: this limits the change to the opening three of five letters, leaving the rest in place
something that rolls over is turned round, so those letters run the other way

parts.note: bread is slang for money, and the rupee is India's currency

explanation.surface: An Indian flatbread rolled up and mashed to feed an infant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian bread' wants to be naan or roti, but bread is money: the rupee. Its first three letters are turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Pureed fruit and vegetables, mashed smooth, are the first solid food given to infants.

clue.text: Tone and Tom running after a ball

indicators.note: a running man is in motion, so his name's letters move about

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a ball is a sphere

explanation.surface: Two boys called Tone and Tom chasing a football.
explanation.walkthrough: Tone looks like a boy's name paired with Tom. The mixed TOM comes after A, as 'after' says.
explanation.definitionFit: The atmosphere of a place or event is its mood or character, as is its tone.

clue.text: Drop baby's cuddly toy

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to give birth to young, as animals drop them
second meaning: a teddy, the stuffed animal children hug

explanation.surface: A baby letting go of its favourite soft toy.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive pulls the two parts together as one scene; split it, and each half is a meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear a child is to give birth, as an animal drops its young; and a teddy is the classic soft toy.

clue.text: Pupil facing questions a setter's put in Old English

indicators.note: something put in a second item ends up inside it

parts.note: ex- means former
taken as written
the setter speaking of what belongs to them says mine
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A student sitting an exam set in Old English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old English' reads as the language of Beowulf, but the two words split and act as a wrapper.
explanation.definitionFit: An examinee is a person being tested, such as a pupil answering the questions on an exam paper.

clue.text: Nursery product displayed in arboretum or used in these borders!

indicators.note: the letters are on show inside the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A plant-nursery product on display in a tree garden, or planted in its flowerbeds.
explanation.walkthrough: Morus is the botanical name for mulberry, the bush of the nursery rhyme 'Here we go round the mulberry bush', so 'Nursery' works both ways; the hidden word sits on the borders between words.
explanation.definitionFit: The mulberry is a tree raised and sold by plant nurseries, and it is also the bush children circle in a nursery rhyme.

clue.text: Big boys' uniform choices for course

parts.note: grown-up boys are men
Uniform is U in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Older schoolboys picking which uniform to wear for a course.
explanation.definitionFit: A menu lists the dishes a diner may pick from for each part of a meal.

clue.text: Mary and Luke modelled small person's headwear

indicators.note: something modelled is shaped like clay into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mary and Luke showing off a child's hat on a catwalk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Modelled' suggests a fashion shoot, but it is the instruction to reshape the two names.
explanation.definitionFit: A yarmulke is the little round skullcap worn by Jewish men and boys, a small piece of headgear.

clue.text: Come up with tips to differentiate the twins, possibly

indicators.note: the tips of a word are its two extremities, its opening and closing letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
the Twins, Gemini, is a sign of the zodiac; 'possibly' says it is one example

explanation.surface: Advice on how to tell identical twins apart.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like telling twins apart; the twins are really Gemini.
explanation.definitionFit: To design something is to devise or invent it, which is coming up with it.

clue.text: Rubbish about hide of Nellie the Elephant being revered by Hindus

indicators.note: about means around, so the first item goes round the second

parts.note: gash is British slang for waste or rubbish

indicators.note: an animal's hide is its outer skin, so only the outside letters are taken

parts.note: the first and last letters of the name
surface padding completing the song title Nellie the Elephant

explanation.surface: Nonsense about the skin of the elephant from the children's song being worshipped in India.
explanation.walkthrough: Nellie the Elephant is a British children's song; the elephant-headed god makes the elephant fit the answer too.
explanation.definitionFit: Ganesh is the elephant-headed Hindu deity of wisdom and new beginnings, a divine being worshipped across India.

clue.text: Scaremongering from 11+? Honestly, it'll make you withstand examination

indicators.note: from the eleventh letter onwards, so everything before it is ignored

parts.note: letters eleven to fourteen, the last four
honestly and truly are synonyms

explanation.surface: Fear spread about the eleven-plus school entrance exam, and whether pupils can stand up to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The 11+ was the British exam deciding entry to grammar school at eleven; here '11+' means the eleventh letter on.
explanation.definitionFit: A story that rings true sounds believable, so it holds up when scrutinised.

clue.text: Diminutive boy and girl vacantly shaking out a bit of ketchup?

indicators.note: shaking jumbles the letters into a new order
diminutive means made smaller, so the word is cut short

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: emptied of its contents, the word keeps only its outer pair of letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Little children shaking a sauce bottle and getting nothing out.
explanation.walkthrough: BOY is cut to BO and mixed with GL.
explanation.definitionFit: A glob is a small blob of thick liquid, the sort of dollop that drops from a sauce bottle; the question mark marks it as an example.

clue.text: Thesaurus entry for boy on seesaw?

indicators.note: an entry is something found within a larger text, here within the word

parts.note: letters three to six of the word

explanation.surface: Looking up a reference book for a word meaning a boy riding a playground seesaw.
explanation.walkthrough: Esau, Jacob's twin in Genesis, is also nearly heard in the word 'seesaw', which is the joke on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Esau is a biblical son of Isaac, so a male name that crosswords use for a boy.

clue.text: Nina managed to keep husband and daughter under control

indicators.note: something managed is handled and arranged, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
H is the standard abbreviation for husband
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Nina managed to keep her husband and daughter in line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under control' looks like a description of the family, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A situation that is being dealt with and is safely handled is said to be in hand.

clue.text: Newspaper article linked boy and girl

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a single news story or report

explanation.surface: A gossip column story connecting two young people.
explanation.definitionFit: A short piece in a paper is called this, and so is a couple who are known to be seeing each other.

clue.text: Salesman had sex endlessly to create another baby boom?

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative
a formal verb for had intercourse

explanation.walkthrough: COPULATED loses its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To repopulate an area is to fill it with people again, which a surge in births would do; the question mark flags the playful example.

clue.text: Living without Charlie Brown

parts.note: earning a crust is making a living

explanation.definitionFit: Rust is a reddish-brown colour, named after the oxide on iron.
